article.title: Why Cheap Money Can Make Expensive Assets
article.framework: Lower Rates → Lower Discount Rate & Financing Cost → Higher Present Values → More Risk-Taking → Higher Asset Prices → Greater Sensitivity to Reversal
article.coreIdea: Interest rates affect asset prices through both mathematics and behavior: lower rates can raise the present value of distant cash flows while also changing financing costs, opportunity costs, leverage, and investors’ willingness to take risk.
article.body:
Imagine an investment that promises to pay you $100 one year from now. If safe investments elsewhere offer almost no return, that future $100 may look attractive today. But if you can earn a high return safely, you would demand a lower price for the same future payment. Nothing about the promised $100 has changed. What changed is the value you place on money received later rather than now.

This simple idea sits behind one of finance's most important links: the relationship between interest rates and asset prices. When rates fall, bonds, stocks, property, and other assets can become more valuable for several reasons. When rates rise, the process can reverse. Yet saying “low rates make markets go up” is too simple. To understand the mechanism, we need to separate valuation, incentives, financing, and expectations.

Start with present value. An asset is valuable partly because of the cash it may generate in the future. Investors translate those future cash flows into today's money using a discount rate. The higher the discount rate, the less a distant payment is worth today. The lower the discount rate, the more valuable that same payment becomes.

This matters especially for assets whose expected profits lie far in the future. Consider two companies. One earns steady cash today. The other is growing rapidly but expects most of its profits ten years from now. When discount rates fall, those distant profits receive a larger boost in present-value terms. This is one reason long-duration assets, including many growth stocks, can be especially sensitive to changes in interest rates.

But valuation mathematics is only the first channel. Interest rates also change opportunity cost. Suppose government bonds offer a safe and attractive return. Investors can earn reasonable income without taking much risk, so risky assets must offer something extra to compete. If safe yields fall sharply, investors may become more willing to buy stocks, corporate bonds, property, or other assets in search of higher returns.

This behavior is sometimes called a search for yield. It does not mean investors suddenly stop caring about risk. Instead, the relative attractiveness of different choices changes. A 5 percent expected return from a risky asset may look unimpressive when safe assets pay 4 percent, but much more appealing when safe assets pay close to zero.

Financing costs create a third channel. Lower interest rates can make borrowing cheaper for households, companies, and investors. A company may find more investment projects profitable when debt costs less. A household may be able to afford a larger mortgage for the same monthly budget. An investor using leverage may be willing to hold a larger position when financing is cheap.

Property markets show how these channels can interact. Lower mortgage rates can increase the amount buyers are able to borrow, supporting housing demand. At the same time, investors may compare rental income with lower bond yields and decide property looks more attractive. If supply cannot respond quickly, stronger demand may appear mainly as higher prices rather than more homes.

This connects to our earlier scarcity framework. Cheap financing can expand purchasing power, but it does not automatically expand the stock of scarce assets. If more money competes for a slowly growing supply of desirable property, land, or other assets, prices can adjust faster than quantities.

There is also a feedback effect. Rising asset prices make existing owners wealthier on paper. Higher collateral values can sometimes support additional borrowing. Strong market returns may attract new investors who fear missing further gains. More demand can then push prices higher again. What began as a change in financial conditions can become a self-reinforcing market narrative.

This is where causality becomes difficult. If stock prices rise after a central bank cuts rates, it is tempting to say the cut caused the rally. But central banks often cut rates because economic conditions are weakening. The same event can therefore contain two signals: easier financial conditions are supportive for valuations, while the reason for the cut may be negative for future profits.

Markets try to price both. A rate cut during a mild slowdown may be welcomed because financing becomes easier while earnings remain resilient. A rate cut during a severe crisis may not lift risky assets immediately because investors are more worried about collapsing profits, defaults, or uncertainty. The direction of rates alone is not enough; the economic context matters.

Expectations make the analysis even more complicated. Asset prices respond not only to today's interest rate but also to what investors expected before the announcement and what they now expect about the future. If everyone already anticipated a rate cut, the cut itself may have little effect. A surprise change in the expected path of rates can matter much more.

This is a useful reminder from our measurement and causality toolbox: markets move on differences between reality and expectations, not simply on whether a number is objectively high or low. “Rates fell” is incomplete information. We also need to ask: compared with what expectation, for how long, and why?

Low rates can also encourage leverage and risk-taking. This may support productive investment, but it can create fragility if borrowers assume cheap financing will last forever. A project that works when debt costs 2 percent may look very different at 6 percent. An investor who can comfortably service leverage during calm markets may be forced to sell when financing costs rise or collateral values fall.

That creates an important asymmetry. Falling rates can gradually encourage positions that depend on low financing costs, while rising rates can expose those dependencies quickly. Asset prices may therefore become more sensitive to rate increases after a long period of cheap money. The first-order effect is cheaper financing; the second-order effect may be a system that has adapted itself to cheap financing.

This connects directly to stock versus flow. A low interest rate is not just a one-day event. If it persists, companies refinance debt, households choose mortgages, investors alter portfolios, and asset prices adjust. Over time, the stock of contracts and positions in the economy becomes shaped by the prevailing rate environment. When that environment changes, adjustment can be painful because old decisions were made under different assumptions.

Today's transferable tool is the Rate Transmission Map. When interest rates change, trace four channels separately. First, valuation: how does the discount rate change present values? Second, alternatives: how attractive are safe assets relative to risky ones? Third, financing: who can borrow more or less cheaply? Fourth, adaptation: what leverage, prices, or business models have accumulated under the old rate regime?

Then add two checks. The Expectations Check asks whether the change was already priced in. The Context Check asks why rates are moving in the first place. These prevent us from treating interest rates as a single mechanical switch.

So when cheap money is associated with expensive assets, the useful question is not simply whether rates are low. Ask which channel is doing the work, what scarcity prevents supply from responding, what risks are being accumulated, and what would happen if the rate environment reversed. That turns a market slogan into an analytical framework.
article.summaryZh:
今天进入 Finance & Economics：为什么“钱更便宜”时，资产反而可能更贵？文章把利率传导拆成四条渠道：Valuation（discount rate 改变未来现金流的 present value）、Alternatives（安全收益下降后出现 search for yield）、Financing（借贷成本改变企业、住房与杠杆决策）、Adaptation（长期低利率会让债务、资产价格和商业模式逐渐适应旧环境）。

这里接回 scarcity：cheap financing 能增加 purchasing power，却不会自动增加土地或住房等稀缺资产的 stock；如果 supply response 很慢，需求更容易体现为价格上涨。也接回 feedback 与 causality：asset price ↑ → collateral/wealth ↑ → borrowing/risk appetite ↑ → demand ↑，但央行降息往往又是因为经济走弱，所以“降息”同时可能包含宽松金融条件和盈利恶化两种信号。

另一个重点是 expectations。市场不是简单对“升息/降息”反应，而是对 actual outcome 与 prior expectation 的差异反应。今天的新工具 Rate Transmission Map 是：Rate Change → Valuation → Alternatives → Financing → Adaptation，再叠加 Expectations Check 与 Context Check。它避免把“降息=股市涨”当成机械规律，并进一步追问旧利率环境下积累了多少 leverage 与脆弱性。

speaking.question: Why do interest rates have such a strong influence on asset prices?
speaking.response: I think interest rates matter through several channels rather than just one. First, lower rates can increase the present value of future cash flows, especially for assets whose profits are expected far in the future. They also make safe investments less attractive, so some investors become more willing to take risk. On top of that, borrowing becomes cheaper for households and companies. However, the effect is not automatic because markets also care about why rates are changing and whether the move was already expected.
expressions: Interest rates matter through several channels rather than just one.
The effect is not automatic because markets also care about why rates are changing.
Markets respond partly to what was already expected.

speaking.question: Can very low interest rates create problems for the economy?
speaking.framework: Immediate benefit → Behavioral adaptation → Leverage → Reversal risk
speaking.response: Yes, although low rates can be useful when an economy needs support. Cheap borrowing can encourage investment and make debt easier to service, but if rates stay low for a long time, people may start making decisions that only work under those conditions. Investors may use more leverage, asset prices may rise, and companies may depend on cheap refinancing. The risk appears when the environment reverses. So I would distinguish the first-order benefit of cheaper financing from the second-order fragility that can build up over time.
expressions: People may start making decisions that only work under those conditions.
The risk appears when the environment reverses.
We should distinguish the first-order benefit from the second-order fragility.
